content.content:
> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Create plugins

> Create custom plugins to extend Claude Code with skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers.

Plugins let you extend Claude Code with custom functionality that can be shared across projects and teams. This guide covers creating your own plugins with skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers.

Looking to install existing plugins? See [Discover and install plugins](/en/discover-plugins). For complete technical specifications, see [Plugins reference](/en/plugins-reference).

## When to use plugins vs standalone configuration

Claude Code supports two ways to add custom skills, agents, and hooks:

| Approach                                                    | Skill names          | Best for                                                                                        |
| :---------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Standalone** (`.claude/` directory)                       | `/hello`             | Personal workflows, project-specific customizations, quick experiments                          |
| **Plugins** (directories with `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`) | `/plugin-name:hello` | Sharing with teammates, distributing to community, versioned releases, reusable across projects |

**Use standalone configuration when**:

* You're customizing Claude Code for a single project
* The configuration is personal and doesn't need to be shared
* You're experimenting with skills or hooks before packaging them
* You want short skill names like `/hello` or `/deploy`

**Use plugins when**:

* You want to share functionality with your team or community
* You need the same skills/agents across multiple projects
* You want version control and easy updates for your extensions
* You're distributing through a marketplace
* You're okay with namespaced skills like `/my-plugin:hello` (namespacing prevents conflicts between plugins)

<Tip>
  Start with standalone configuration in `.claude/` for quick iteration, then [convert to a plugin](#convert-existing-configurations-to-plugins) when you're ready to share.
</Tip>

## Quickstart

This quickstart walks you through creating a plugin with a custom skill. You'll create a manifest (the configuration file that defines your plugin), add a skill, and test it locally using the `--plugin-dir` flag.

### Prerequisites

* Claude Code [installed and authenticated](/en/quickstart#step-1-install-claude-code)
* Claude Code version 1.0.33 or later (run `claude --version` to check)

<Note>
  If you don't see the `/plugin` command, update Claude Code to the latest version. See [Troubleshooting](/en/troubleshooting) for upgrade instructions.
</Note>

### Create your first plugin

<Steps>
  <Step title="Create the plugin directory">
    Every plugin lives in its own directory containing a manifest and your skills, agents, or hooks. Create one now:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    mkdir my-first-plugin
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create the plugin manifest">
    The manifest file at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` defines your plugin's identity: its name, description, and version. Claude Code uses this metadata to display your plugin in the plugin manager.

    Create the `.claude-plugin` directory inside your plugin folder:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    mkdir my-first-plugin/.claude-plugin
    ```

    Then create `my-first-plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` with this content:

    ```json my-first-plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json theme={null}
    {
    "name": "my-first-plugin",
    "description": "A greeting plugin to learn the basics",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "author": {
    "name": "Your Name"
    }
    }
    ```

    | Field         | Purpose                                                                                                |
    | :------------ | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    | `name`        | Unique identifier and skill namespace. Skills are prefixed with this (e.g., `/my-first-plugin:hello`). |
    | `description` | Shown in the plugin manager when browsing or installing plugins.                                       |
    | `version`     | Track releases using [semantic versioning](/en/plugins-reference#version-management).                  |
    | `author`      | Optional. Helpful for attribution.                                                                     |

    For additional fields like `homepage`, `repository`, and `license`, see the [full manifest schema](/en/plugins-reference#plugin-manifest-schema).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add a skill">
    Skills live in the `skills/` directory. Each skill is a folder containing a `SKILL.md` file. The folder name becomes the skill name, prefixed with the plugin's namespace (`hello/` in a plugin named `my-first-plugin` creates `/my-first-plugin:hello`).

    Create a skill directory in your plugin folder:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    mkdir -p my-first-plugin/skills/hello
    ```

    Then create `my-first-plugin/skills/hello/SKILL.md` with this content:

    ```markdown my-first-plugin/skills/hello/SKILL.md theme={null}
    ---
    description: Greet the user with a friendly message
    disable-model-invocation: true
    ---

    Greet the user warmly and ask how you can help them today.
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Test your plugin">
    Run Claude Code with the `--plugin-dir` flag to load your plugin:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    claude --plugin-dir ./my-first-plugin
    ```

    Once Claude Code starts, try your new skill:

    ```shell  theme={null}
    /my-first-plugin:hello
    ```

    You'll see Claude respond with a greeting. Run `/help` to see your skill listed under the plugin namespace.

    <Note>
      **Why namespacing?** Plugin skills are always namespaced (like `/greet:hello`) to prevent conflicts when multiple plugins have skills with the same name.

      To change the namespace prefix, update the `name` field in `plugin.json`.
    </Note>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add skill arguments">
    Make your skill dynamic by accepting user input. The `$ARGUMENTS` placeholder captures any text the user provides after the skill name.

    Update your `SKILL.md` file:

    ```markdown my-first-plugin/skills/hello/SKILL.md theme={null}
    ---
    description: Greet the user with a personalized message
    ---

    # Hello Skill

    Greet the user named "$ARGUMENTS" warmly and ask how you can help them today. Make the greeting personal and encouraging.
    ```

    Run `/reload-plugins` to pick up the changes, then try the skill with your name:

    ```shell  theme={null}
    /my-first-plugin:hello Alex
    ```

    Claude will greet you by name. For more on passing arguments to skills, see [Skills](/en/skills#pass-arguments-to-skills).
  </Step>
</Steps>

You've successfully created and tested a plugin with these key components:

* **Plugin manifest** (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`): describes your plugin's metadata
* **Skills directory** (`skills/`): contains your custom skills
* **Skill arguments** (`$ARGUMENTS`): captures user input for dynamic behavior

<Tip>
  The `--plugin-dir` flag is useful for development and testing. When you're ready to share your plugin with others, see [Create and distribute a plugin marketplace](/en/plugin-marketplaces).
</Tip>

## Plugin structure overview

You've created a plugin with a skill, but plugins can include much more: custom agents, hooks, MCP servers, and LSP servers.

<Warning>
  **Common mistake**: Don't put `commands/`, `agents/`, `skills/`, or `hooks/` inside the `.claude-plugin/` directory. Only `plugin.json` goes inside `.claude-plugin/`. All other directories must be at the plugin root level.
</Warning>

| Directory         | Location    | Purpose                                                                        |
| :---------------- | :---------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.claude-plugin/` | Plugin root | Contains `plugin.json` manifest (optional if components use default locations) |
| `commands/`       | Plugin root | Skills as Markdown files                                                       |
| `agents/`         | Plugin root | Custom agent definitions                                                       |
| `skills/`         | Plugin root | Agent Skills with `SKILL.md` files                                             |
| `hooks/`          | Plugin root | Event handlers in `hooks.json`                                                 |
| `.mcp.json`       | Plugin root | MCP server configurations                                                      |
| `.lsp.json`       | Plugin root | LSP server configurations for code intelligence                                |
| `settings.json`   | Plugin root | Default [settings](/en/settings) applied when the plugin is enabled            |

<Note>
  **Next steps**: Ready to add more features? Jump to [Develop more complex plugins](#develop-more-complex-plugins) to add agents, hooks, MCP servers, and LSP servers. For complete technical specifications of all plugin components, see [Plugins reference](/en/plugins-reference).
</Note>

## Develop more complex plugins

Once you're comfortable with basic plugins, you can create more sophisticated extensions.

### Add Skills to your plugin

Plugins can include [Agent Skills](/en/skills) to extend Claude's capabilities. Skills are model-invoked: Claude automatically uses them based on the task context.

Add a `skills/` directory at your plugin root with Skill folders containing `SKILL.md` files:

```text  theme={null}
my-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
└── skills/
    └── code-review/
        └── SKILL.md
```

Each `SKILL.md` needs frontmatter with `name` and `description` fields, followed by instructions:

```yaml  theme={null}
---
name: code-review
description: Reviews code for best practices and potential issues. Use when reviewing code, checking PRs, or analyzing code quality.
---

When reviewing code, check for:
1. Code organization and structure
2. Error handling
3. Security concerns
4. Test coverage
```

After installing the plugin, run `/reload-plugins` to load the Skills. For complete Skill authoring guidance including progressive disclosure and tool restrictions, see [Agent Skills](/en/skills).

### Add LSP servers to your plugin

<Tip>
  For common languages like TypeScript, Python, and Rust, install the pre-built LSP plugins from the official marketplace. Create custom LSP plugins only when you need support for languages not already covered.
</Tip>

LSP (Language Server Protocol) plugins give Claude real-time code intelligence. If you need to support a language that doesn't have an official LSP plugin, you can create your own by adding an `.lsp.json` file to your plugin:

```json .lsp.json theme={null}
{
  "go": {
    "command": "gopls",
    "args": ["serve"],
    "extensionToLanguage": {
      ".go": "go"
    }
  }
}
```

Users installing your plugin must have the language server binary installed on their machine.

For complete LSP configuration options, see [LSP servers](/en/plugins-reference#lsp-servers).

### Ship default settings with your plugin

Plugins can include a `settings.json` file at the plugin root to apply default configuration when the plugin is enabled. Currently, only the `agent` key is supported.

Setting `agent` activates one of the plugin's [custom agents](/en/sub-agents) as the main thread, applying its system prompt, tool restrictions, and model. This lets a plugin change how Claude Code behaves by default when enabled.

```json settings.json theme={null}
{
  "agent": "security-reviewer"
}
```

This example activates the `security-reviewer` agent defined in the plugin's `agents/` directory. Settings from `settings.json` take priority over `settings` declared in `plugin.json`. Unknown keys are silently ignored.

### Organize complex plugins

For plugins with many components, organize your directory structure by functionality. For complete directory layouts and organization patterns, see [Plugin directory structure](/en/plugins-reference#plugin-directory-structure).

### Test your plugins locally

Use the `--plugin-dir` flag to test plugins during development. This loads your plugin directly without requiring installation.

```bash  theme={null}
claude --plugin-dir ./my-plugin
```

When a `--plugin-dir` plugin has the same name as an installed marketplace plugin, the local copy takes precedence for that session. This lets you test changes to a plugin you already have installed without uninstalling it first. Marketplace plugins force-enabled by managed settings are the only exception and cannot be overridden.

As you make changes to your plugin, run `/reload-plugins` to pick up the updates without restarting. This reloads commands, skills, agents, hooks, plugin MCP servers, and plugin LSP servers. Test your plugin components:

* Try your skills with `/plugin-name:skill-name`
* Check that agents appear in `/agents`
* Verify hooks work as expected

<Tip>
  You can load multiple plugins at once by specifying the flag multiple times:

  ```bash  theme={null}
  claude --plugin-dir ./plugin-one --plugin-dir ./plugin-two
  ```
</Tip>

### Debug plugin issues

If your plugin isn't working as expected:

1. **Check the structure**: Ensure your directories are at the plugin root, not inside `.claude-plugin/`
2. **Test components individually**: Check each command, agent, and hook separately
3. **Use validation and debugging tools**: See [Debugging and development tools](/en/plugins-reference#debugging-and-development-tools) for CLI commands and troubleshooting techniques

### Share your plugins

When your plugin is ready to share:

1. **Add documentation**: Include a `README.md` with installation and usage instructions
2. **Version your plugin**: Use [semantic versioning](/en/plugins-reference#version-management) in your `plugin.json`
3. **Create or use a marketplace**: Distribute through [plugin marketplaces](/en/plugin-marketplaces) for installation
4. **Test with others**: Have team members test the plugin before wider distribution

Once your plugin is in a marketplace, others can install it using the instructions in [Discover and install plugins](/en/discover-plugins).

### Submit your plugin to the official marketplace

To submit a plugin to the official Anthropic marketplace, use one of the in-app submission forms:

* **Claude.ai**: [claude.ai/settings/plugins/submit](https://claude.ai/settings/plugins/submit)
* **Console**: [platform.claude.com/plugins/submit](https://platform.claude.com/plugins/submit)

<Note>
  For complete technical specifications, debugging techniques, and distribution strategies, see [Plugins reference](/en/plugins-reference).
</Note>

## Convert existing configurations to plugins

If you already have skills or hooks in your `.claude/` directory, you can convert them into a plugin for easier sharing and distribution.

### Migration steps

<Steps>
  <Step title="Create the plugin structure">
    Create a new plugin directory:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    mkdir -p my-plugin/.claude-plugin
    ```

    Create the manifest file at `my-plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:

    ```json my-plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json theme={null}
    {
      "name": "my-plugin",
      "description": "Migrated from standalone configuration",
      "version": "1.0.0"
    }
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Copy your existing files">
    Copy your existing configurations to the plugin directory:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    # Copy commands
    cp -r .claude/commands my-plugin/

    # Copy agents (if any)
    cp -r .claude/agents my-plugin/

    # Copy skills (if any)
    cp -r .claude/skills my-plugin/
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Migrate hooks">
    If you have hooks in your settings, create a hooks directory:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    mkdir my-plugin/hooks
    ```

    Create `my-plugin/hooks/hooks.json` with your hooks configuration. Copy the `hooks` object from your `.claude/settings.json` or `settings.local.json`, since the format is the same. The command receives hook input as JSON on stdin, so use `jq` to extract the file path:

    ```json my-plugin/hooks/hooks.json theme={null}
    {
      "hooks": {
        "PostToolUse": [
          {
            "matcher": "Write|Edit",
            "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npm run lint:fix" }]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Test your migrated plugin">
    Load your plugin to verify everything works:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    claude --plugin-dir ./my-plugin
    ```

    Test each component: run your commands, check agents appear in `/agents`, and verify hooks trigger correctly.
  </Step>
</Steps>

### What changes when migrating

| Standalone (`.claude/`)       | Plugin                           |
| :---------------------------- | :------------------------------- |
| Only available in one project | Can be shared via marketplaces   |
| Files in `.claude/commands/`  | Files in `plugin-name/commands/` |
| Hooks in `settings.json`      | Hooks in `hooks/hooks.json`      |
| Must manually copy to share   | Install with `/plugin install`   |

<Note>
  After migrating, you can remove the original files from `.claude/` to avoid duplicates. The plugin version will take precedence when loaded.
</Note>

## Next steps

Now that you understand Claude Code's plugin system, here are suggested paths for different goals:

### For plugin users

* [Discover and install plugins](/en/discover-plugins): browse marketplaces and install plugins
* [Configure team marketplaces](/en/discover-plugins#configure-team-marketplaces): set up repository-level plugins for your team

### For plugin developers

* [Create and distribute a marketplace](/en/plugin-marketplaces): package and share your plugins
* [Plugins reference](/en/plugins-reference): complete technical specifications
* Dive deeper into specific plugin components:
  * [Skills](/en/skills): skill development details
  * [Subagents](/en/sub-agents): agent configuration and capabilities
  * [Hooks](/en/hooks): event handling and automation
  * [MCP](/en/mcp): external tool integration

1→# pskoett-ai-skills
     2→
     3→A collection of skills for AI agents. Follows the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification).
     4→This repository is my personal skill testing ground.
     5→
     6→## Install
     7→
     8→```bash
     9→npx skills add pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills
    10→```
    11→
    12→## Structure
    13→
    14→```
    15→skills/
    16→  skill-name/
    17→    SKILL.md         # Required - skill definition with YAML frontmatter
    18→    scripts/         # Optional - executable code
    19→    references/      # Optional - documentation loaded on demand
    20→    assets/          # Optional - templates, images, data files
    21→```
    22→
    23→## Skills
    24→
    25→| Skill | Description |
    26→|-------|-------------|
    27→| [agent-teams-simplify-and-harden](skills/agent-teams-simplify-and-harden/) | Implementation + audit loop using parallel agent teams with structured simplify, harden, and document passes |
    28→| [context-surfing](skills/context-surfing/) | Monitors context window health and rides peak context quality for maximum output fidelity during multi-step execution |
    29→| [dx-data-navigator](skills/dx-data-navigator/) | Query DX Data Cloud for developer productivity metrics, DORA metrics, PR/deployment data, and engineering analytics |
    30→| [intent-framed-agent](skills/intent-framed-agent/) | Captures a lightweight intent contract at execution start and monitors coding-task drift until resolution |
    31→| [plan-interview](skills/plan-interview/) | Runs a structured interview before planning non-trivial implementations |
    32→| [self-improvement](skills/self-improvement/) | Captures learnings and errors with hook-based activation and automatic skill extraction |
    33→| [simplify-and-harden](skills/simplify-and-harden/) | Post-completion self-review that runs simplify, harden, and micro-documentation passes before signaling done |
    34→
    35→## Experimental (CI Skills)
    36→
    37→These skills are experimental and currently part of the testing ground setup.
    38→
    39→| Skill | Description |
    40→|-------|-------------|
    41→| [self-improvement-ci](skills/self-improvement-ci/) | CI-only self-improvement workflow for recurring failure-pattern capture using gh-aw |
    42→| [simplify-and-harden-ci](skills/simplify-and-harden-ci/) | CI-only simplify/harden workflow for pull requests using gh-aw with headless scan/report gates |
    43→
    44→## Skill Pipeline
    45→
    46→Each skill prevents a distinct failure mode:
    47→
    48→| Skill | Failure it prevents |
    49→|-------|-------------------|
    50→| `plan-interview` | Building the wrong thing |
    51→| `intent-framed-agent` | Scope creep during execution |
    52→| `context-surfing` | Degraded-context corruption |
    53→| `simplify-and-harden` | Shipping rough/insecure code |
    54→| `self-improvement` | Repeating the same mistakes |
    55→
    56→### Lifecycle
    57→
    58→```
    59→[plan-interview] → [intent-framed-agent] ⟂ [context-surfing] → [simplify-and-harden] → [self-improvement]
    60→                                          ↑   concurrent    ↑
    61→```
    62→
    63→**Stage 1 — Planning** (manual gate): `plan-interview` runs a structured interview and produces a plan file in `docs/plans/`. This is the only skill that requires explicit invocation (`/plan-interview`). Downstream skills activate automatically when present, but each works independently if earlier stages are skipped.
    64→
    65→**Stage 2 — Execution** (concurrent monitoring): `intent-framed-agent` captures the intent frame and monitors *scope* drift. `context-surfing` monitors *context quality* drift. Both run simultaneously. If both fire at once, context-surfing's exit takes precedence — degraded context makes scope checks unreliable.
    66→
    67→**Stage 3 — Review** (post-completion): `simplify-and-harden` runs three passes (simplify, harden, document) on the completed work.
    68→
    69→**Stage 4 — Learning** (automatic): `self-improvement` captures recurring patterns from the session and promotes them to project-level instruction files.
    70→
    71→### Artifacts at each stage
    72→
    73→| Stage | Artifact | Location |
    74→|-------|----------|----------|
    75→| Planning | Plan file | `docs/plans/plan-NNN-<slug>.md` |
    76→| Execution | Intent frame | Emitted in session output |
    77→| Execution | Handoff file (on drift exit) | `.context-surfing/handoff-<slug>-<timestamp>.md` |
    78→| Review | Structured YAML summary | Appended to task output |
    79→| Learning | Learning entries | `.learnings/LEARNINGS.md`, `ERRORS.md`, `FEATURE_REQUESTS.md` |
    80→
    81→### Pipeline depth
    82→
    83→Every skill works standalone. The pipeline is the recommended combination, not a hard dependency — each skill silently adapts when upstream artifacts are absent.
    84→
    85→Match depth to complexity:
    86→
    87→| Task | Skills |
    88→|------|--------|
    89→| Trivial (typo fix, rename) | None |
    90→| Small (isolated bug fix) | `simplify-and-harden` |
    91→| Medium (feature, multi-file) | `intent-framed-agent` + `simplify-and-harden` |
    92→| Large (refactor, new architecture) | Full pipeline |
    93→| Long-running (multi-session) | Full pipeline — `context-surfing` is critical |
    94→
    95→## Usage
    96→
    97→To use a skill, add it to your agent's configuration or reference it directly.
    98→
    99→### Hook Setup
   100→
   101→Several skills support automatic activation via hooks. Add to `.claude/settings.json`:
   102→
   103→```json
   104→{
   105→  "hooks": {
   106→    "UserPromptSubmit": [{
   107→      "matcher": "",
   108→      "hooks": [
   109→        {
   110→          "type": "command",
   111→          "command": "./skills/self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh"
   112→        },
   113→        {
   114→          "type": "command",
   115→          "command": "./skills/context-surfing/scripts/handoff-checker.sh"
   116→        }
   117→      ]
   118→    }]
   119→  }
   120→}
   121→```
   122→
   123→| Hook Script | Skill | Purpose |
   124→|-------------|-------|---------|
   125→| `self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh` | self-improvement | Reminds to evaluate learnings after tasks |
   126→| `context-surfing/scripts/handoff-checker.sh` | context-surfing | Detects unread handoff files from previous context exits |
   127→
   128→Both hooks are lightweight (~50-100 tokens) and skip silently when not applicable.
   129→
   130→## Contributing
   131→
   132→Feel free to submit PRs with new skills or improvements to existing ones.
   133→

1→---
     2→name: plan-interview
     3→description: |
     4→  Ensures alignment between user and Claude during feature/spec planning through a structured interview process.
     5→
     6→  Use this skill when the user invokes /plan-interview before implementing a new feature, refactoring, or any non-trivial implementation task. The skill runs an upfront interview to gather requirements across technical constraints, scope boundaries, risk tolerance, and success criteria before any codebase exploration.
     7→
     8→  Do NOT use this skill for: pure research/exploration tasks, simple bug fixes, or when the user just wants standard planning without the interview process.
     9→---
    10→
    11→# Plan Interview Skill
    12→
    13→## Install
    14→
    15→```bash
    16→npx skills add pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills/skills/plan-interview
    17→```
    18→
    19→## Purpose
    20→
    21→Run a structured requirements interview before planning implementation. This ensures alignment between you and the user by gathering explicit requirements rather than making assumptions.
    22→
    23→## When Invoked
    24→
    25→User calls `/plan-interview <task description>`.
    26→
    27→**Skip this skill** if the task is purely research/exploration (not implementation).
    28→
    29→## Interview Process
    30→
    31→### Phase 1: Upfront Interview (Before Exploration)
    32→
    33→Interview the user using `AskUserQuestion` in **thematic batches of 2-3 questions** when the provider supports it. For providers like GitHub Copilot without an AskUser tool, ask the same questions directly in chat and pause for responses before continuing.
    34→
    35→#### Required Question Domains
    36→
    37→Cover ALL four domains before proceeding:
    38→
    39→1. **Technical Constraints**
    40→   - Performance requirements
    41→   - Compatibility needs
    42→   - Existing patterns to follow
    43→   - Architecture understanding (if codebase is unfamiliar)
    44→
    45→2. **Scope Boundaries**
    46→   - What's explicitly OUT of scope
    47→   - MVP vs full vision
    48→   - Dependencies on other work
    49→
    50→3. **Risk Tolerance**
    51→   - Acceptable tradeoffs (speed vs quality)
    52→   - Tech debt tolerance
    53→   - Breaking change acceptance
    54→
    55→4. **Success Criteria**
    56→   - How will we know it's done?
    57→   - What defines "working correctly"?
    58→   - Testing/validation requirements
    59→
    60→#### Question Generation
    61→
    62→- Generate questions **dynamically** based on the task - no fixed template
    63→- Group related questions into thematic batches
    64→- **2-3 questions per batch** (do not exceed)
    65→- Continue until you have **actionable specificity** (can describe concrete implementation steps)
    66→
    67→#### Planning Depth Calibration
    68→
    69→Before leaving the interview phase, classify the task and choose a planning depth:
    70→
    71→- **Simple/trivial** (small bug fix, isolated change): minimal plan, at most 1 refinement pass
    72→- **Moderate** (feature work in known area): standard plan, usually 1-2 refinement passes
    73→- **Complex/high-risk** (multi-file, new architecture, unfamiliar codebase, migrations, auth, concurrency): deep plan with iterative refinement until improvements flatten
    74→
    75→Let the user override this (`fast` vs `deep`) if they have a clear preference.
    76→
    77→#### Handling Edge Cases
    78→
    79→| Scenario | Action |
    80→|----------|--------|
    81→| Contradictory requirements | Make a recommendation with rationale, ask for confirmation |
    82→| User pivots requirements | Restart interview fresh with new direction |
    83→| Interrupted session | Ask user: continue where we left off or restart? |
    84→
    85→#### Anti-Patterns to Avoid
    86→
    87→- Do NOT ask variations of the same question
    88→- Do NOT make major assumptions without asking
    89→- Do NOT over-engineer plans for simple tasks
    90→
    91→### Phase 2: Codebase Exploration
    92→
    93→After interview completes, explore the codebase to understand:
    94→- Existing patterns relevant to the task
    95→- Files that will be affected
    96→- Integration points
    97→- Potential risks
    98→
    99→For complex or unfamiliar projects, do a brief context refresh before deep planning:
   100→- Re-read `AGENTS.md` and `README.md` if present and relevant
   101→- Identify the current architecture boundaries and conventions before refining the plan
   102→- If the session was interrupted or context drifted, refresh these again before another refinement round
   103→
   104→### Phase 3: Plan Generation
   105→
   106→Write plan to `docs/plans/plan-NNN-<slug>.md` where NNN is sequential.
   107→
   108→Use a **draft -> refine** workflow. Stay in plan space while you are still finding material improvements. Planning tokens are usually much cheaper than implementation tokens for non-trivial work.
   109→
   110→#### Draft First, Then Refine
   111→
   112→1. Create a draft plan from the interview + exploration results.
   113→2. Run iterative refinement passes before asking for approval (depth based on task complexity).
   114→3. Present the refined plan for user review.
   115→
   116→#### Iterative Plan Refinement Loop (Before User Review)
   117→
   118→Run 1..N refinement passes depending on complexity. For each pass:
   119→
   120→1. **Fresh-eyes start (mandatory):** Re-read the interview answers, constraints, success criteria, and the current draft plan with "fresh eyes" before revising anything.
   121→2. Check for contradictions, missing edge cases, integration risks, and vague implementation steps.
   122→3. Improve architecture, sequencing, and reliability where it clearly helps users.
   123→4. Strengthen the testing and validation plan (unit + integration/e2e where applicable, plus useful diagnostics/logging).
   124→5. Verify feature preservation:
   125→   - **Do NOT oversimplify**
   126→   - **Do NOT remove agreed features or functionality** unless the user explicitly approves a scope reduction
   127→6. Record a short per-pass summary: what changed and why.
   128→
   129→Stop iterating when any of the following is true:
   130→- Two consecutive passes produce no material improvements
   131→- Changes are only wording/style with no effect on execution quality
   132→- The task is simple and the plan is already actionable
   133→- The user asks to stop and proceed
   134→
   135→#### Optional: Multi-Plan Synthesis ("Best of All Worlds")
   136→
   137→If the user provides multiple competing plans (from different models or prior iterations):
   138→
   139→- Compare them honestly against the current plan
   140→- Extract the best ideas, tradeoffs, and risk mitigations
   141→- Merge them into a single canonical plan that preserves agreed scope
   142→- Prefer showing **git-diff style changes** to the existing plan when the user asks for revision output
   143→
   144→Reusable prompt templates for the refinement loop and multi-plan synthesis live in `references/iterative-plan-refinement-prompts.md`.
   145→
   146→#### Required Elements
   147→
   148→Every plan MUST include:
   149→
   150→```markdown
   151→## Success Criteria
   152→[Clear definition of done from interview]
   153→
   154→## Risk Assessment
   155→[What could go wrong + mitigations]
   156→
   157→## Affected Files/Areas
   158→[Which parts of codebase will be touched]
   159→
   160→## Test Strategy
   161→[Unit tests, integration tests, and e2e tests/scripts where applicable; include key scenarios, failure modes, and fixtures/mocks]
   162→
   163→## Validation and Diagnostics
   164→[How to verify the feature works after implementation; include detailed logging/diagnostics expectations in tests/scripts when useful for debugging]
   165→
   166→## Open Questions
   167→[Uncertainties to resolve during implementation]
   168→- [ ] Question 1 - [Blocks implementation / Can proceed]
   169→- [ ] Question 2 - [Blocks implementation / Can proceed]
   170→
   171→## Implementation Checklist
   172→- [ ] Step 1
   173→- [ ] Step 2
   174→...
   175→```
   176→
   177→#### Optional Elements
   178→
   179→Include when relevant:
   180→
   181→- **Rejected Alternatives**: Only for major architectural decisions
   182→- **Decision Tree**: Only when multiple valid approaches exist
   183→- **Visual Diagrams**: ASCII or Mermaid when helpful for understanding
   184→
   185→#### Constraints
   186→
   187→- **No time estimates** - describe what needs doing, not how long
   188→- **No length limits** - plan should match task complexity
   189→- **No silent scope reduction** - do not drop agreed features to make the plan "cleaner"
   190→- **Don't over-iterate simple work** - use the planning depth calibration above
   191→- Freeform structure beyond required elements
   192→
   193→### Phase 4: Post-Approval
   194→
   195→When user approves the plan:
   196→
   197→1. **Auto-start implementation** immediately (no "proceed" confirmation needed)
   198→2. Populate `TodoWrite` with checklist items
   199→3. At **natural breakpoints** (significant decisions), compare progress to plan
   200→
   201→## Fast Mode
   202→
   203→If user wants quick planning, use **draft + refine**:
   204→
   205→1. Perform task-focused codebase search
   206→2. Generate draft plan
   207→3. Run abbreviated interview to refine
   208→4. Run exactly one **fresh-eyes** refinement pass (preserve functionality, tighten steps, add test/validation coverage)
   209→
   210→## Resume Support
   211→
   212→If a partial plan exists in `docs/plans/`:
   213→
   214→```
   215→AskUserQuestion: "I found an existing partial plan. Would you like to:"
   216→- "Continue the interview"
   217→- "Resume plan drafting/refinement"
   218→- "Review current plan and finalize"
   219→- "Start fresh with a new plan"
   220→```
   221→
   222→If resuming refinement, first summarize the current plan state and the most recent refinement changes, then continue with the fresh-eyes refinement loop.
   223→
   224→## Interoperability with Other Skills
   225→
   226→### What this skill consumes
   227→- **From the user:** Task description, requirements, and answers to interview questions.
   228→- **From the codebase:** Existing patterns, architecture, and conventions discovered during exploration.
   229→- **From context-surfing handoff files (on resume):** If a previous session exited due to context drift, the handoff file in `.context-surfing/` provides the re-entry point and remaining work for replanning.
   230→
   231→### What this skill produces
   232→- **Plan file** (`docs/plans/plan-NNN-<slug>.md`) — consumed by intent-framed-agent as context for the intent frame, and by context-surfing as part of the wave anchor. Copied verbatim into handoff files on drift exit.
   233→- **Planning depth classification** — informs how many skills to activate (see pipeline depth table in README).
   234→
   235→### Pipeline position
   236→1. `plan-interview` (requirements and plan generation — you are here)
   237→2. `intent-framed-agent` (execution contract + scope drift monitoring)
   238→3. `context-surfing` (context quality monitoring — runs concurrently with intent-framed-agent)
   239→4. `simplify-and-harden` (post-completion quality/security pass)
   240→5. `self-improvement` (capture recurring patterns and promote durable rules)
   241→
   242→## Example
   243→
   244→```
   245→User: /plan-interview Add OAuth authentication to the API
   246→
   247→Claude: I'll help you plan the OAuth authentication feature. Let me gather
   248→        requirements first.
   249→
   250→[AskUserQuestion - Scope batch]
   251→1. Which OAuth providers need to be supported (Google, GitHub, etc.)?
   252→2. Is this replacing existing auth or adding alongside it?
   253→
   254→[Copilot guidance: ask the same two questions in chat and wait for responses]
   255→
   256→User: Google and GitHub. Adding alongside existing JWT auth.
   257→
   258→[AskUserQuestion - Technical batch]
   259→1. Should OAuth tokens be stored in the existing session table or separately?
   260→2. Any specific callback URL constraints from your hosting setup?
   261→
   262→User: Separate table. We're on Vercel so callback URLs need to be configured per environment.
   263→
   264→[AskUserQuestion - Risk/Success batch]
   265→1. What's the acceptable degradation if an OAuth provider is down?
   266→2. How should we handle users who already exist with the same email?
   267→
   268→User: Fall back to standard login. Link accounts by email if user confirms.
   269→
   270→Claude: [Explores codebase for auth patterns, session handling, database schema]
   271→
   272→Claude: [Writes docs/plans/plan-003-oauth-authentication.md]
   273→
   274→        Plan created. The main decision point is whether to use Passport.js
   275→        or implement OAuth flows directly - I've documented both approaches
   276→        with tradeoffs. Ready to review?
   277→
   278→User: Looks good, go with Passport.js
   279→
   280→Claude: [Auto-starts implementation with TodoWrite tracking]
   281→```
   282→

     2→name: intent-framed-agent
     3→description: "Frames coding-agent work sessions with explicit intent capture and drift monitoring. Use when a session transitions from planning/Q&A to implementation for coding tasks, refactors, feature builds, bug fixes, or other multi-step execution where scope drift is a risk."
     4→---
     5→
     6→# Intent Framed Agent
     7→
     8→## Install
     9→
    10→```bash
    11→npx skills add pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills
    12→```
    13→
    14→```bash
    15→npx skills add pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills/skills/intent-framed-agent
    16→```
    17→
    18→## Purpose
    19→
    20→This skill turns implicit intent into an explicit, trackable artifact at the
    21→moment execution starts. It creates a lightweight intent contract, watches for
    22→scope drift while work is in progress, and closes each intent with a short
    23→resolution record.
    24→
    25→## Scope (Important)
    26→
    27→Use this skill for coding tasks only. It is designed for implementation work
    28→that changes executable code.
    29→
    30→Do not use it for general-agent activities such as:
    31→- broad research
    32→- planning-only conversations
    33→- documentation-only work
    34→- operational/admin tasks with no coding implementation
    35→
    36→For trivial edits (for example, simple renames or typo fixes), skip the full
    37→intent frame.
    38→
    39→## Trigger
    40→
    41→Activate at the planning-to-execution transition for non-trivial coding work.
    42→
    43→Common cues:
    44→- User says: "go ahead", "implement this", "let's start building"
    45→- Agent is about to move from discussion into code changes
    46→
    47→## Workflow
    48→
    49→### Phase 1: Intent Capture
    50→
    51→At execution start, emit:
    52→
    53→```markdown
    54→## Intent Frame #N
    55→
    56→**Outcome:** [One sentence. What does done look like?]
    57→**Approach:** [How we will implement it. Key decisions.]
    58→**Constraints:** [Out-of-scope boundaries.]
    59→**Success criteria:** [How we verify completion.]
    60→**Estimated complexity:** [Small / Medium / Large]
    61→```
    62→
    63→Rules:
    64→- Keep each field to 1-2 sentences.
    65→- Ask for confirmation before coding:
    66→  - `Does this capture what we are doing? Anything to adjust before I start?`
    67→- Do not proceed until the user confirms or adjusts.
    68→
    69→### Phase 2: Intent Monitor
    70→
    71→During execution, monitor for drift at natural boundaries:
    72→- before touching a new area/file
    73→- before starting a new logical work unit
    74→- when current action feels tangential
    75→
    76→Drift examples:
    77→- work outside stated scope
    78→- approach changes with no explicit pivot
    79→- new features/refactors outside constraints
    80→- solving a different problem than the stated outcome
    81→
    82→When detected, emit:
    83→
    84→```markdown
    85→## Intent Check #N
    86→
    87→This looks like it may be moving outside the stated intent.
    88→
    89→**Stated outcome:** [From active frame]
    90→**Current action:** [What is happening]
    91→**Question:** Is this a deliberate pivot or accidental scope creep?
    92→```
    93→
    94→If pivot is intentional, update the active intent frame and continue. If not,
    95→return to the original scope.
    96→
    97→### Phase 3: Intent Resolution
    98→
    99→When work under the active intent ends, emit:
   100→
   101→```markdown
   102→## Intent Resolution #N
   103→
   104→**Outcome:** [Fulfilled / Partially fulfilled / Pivoted / Abandoned]
   105→**What was delivered:** [Brief actual output]
   106→**Pivots:** [Any acknowledged changes, or None]
   107→**Open items:** [Remaining in-scope items, or None]
   108→```
   109→
   110→Resolution is preferred but optional if the session ends abruptly.
   111→
   112→## Multi-Intent Sessions
   113→
   114→One session can contain multiple intent frames.
   115→
   116→Rules:
   117→1. Resolve current intent before opening the next.
   118→2. If user changes direction mid-task, resolve current intent as
   119→   `Abandoned` or `Pivoted`, then open a new frame.
   120→3. Drift checks always target the currently active frame.
   121→4. Number frames sequentially within the session (`#1`, `#2`, ...).
   122→5. Constraints do not carry forward unless explicitly restated.
   123→
   124→## Entire CLI Integration
   125→
   126→Entire CLI: https://github.com/entireio/cli
   127→
   128→When tool access is available, detect Entire at activation:
   129→
   130→```bash
   131→entire status 2>/dev/null
   132→```
   133→
   134→- If it succeeds, mention that intent records will be captured in the session
   135→  transcript on the checkpoint branch.
   136→- If unavailable/failing, continue silently. Do not block execution and do not
   137→  nag about installation.
   138→
   139→Copilot/chat fallback:
   140→- If command execution is unavailable, skip detection and continue with the
   141→  same intent workflow in chat output.
   142→
   143→## Guardrails
   144→
   145→- Keep it lightweight; avoid long prose.
   146→- Do not over-trigger on trivial tasks.
   147→- Do not interrupt on every small step.
   148→- Treat acknowledged pivots as valid.
   149→- Preserve exact structured block headers/fields for parseability.
   150→
   151→## Interoperability with Other Skills
   152→
   153→Use this skill as the front-door alignment layer for non-trivial coding work:
   154→1. `plan-interview` (optional, for requirement shaping)
   155→2. `intent-framed-agent` (execution contract + scope drift monitoring)
   156→3. `context-surfing` (context quality monitoring — runs concurrently with intent-framed-agent during execution)
   157→4. `simplify-and-harden` (post-completion quality/security pass)
   158→5. `self-improvement` (capture recurring patterns and promote durable rules)
   159→
   160→### Relationship with context-surfing
   161→
   162→Both skills are live during execution. They monitor different failure modes:
   163→
   164→- **intent-framed-agent** monitors *scope* drift — is the agent doing the right
   165→  thing? It fires structured Intent Checks when work moves outside the stated
   166→  outcome.
   167→- **context-surfing** monitors *context quality* drift — is the agent still
   168→  capable of doing it well? It fires when the agent's own coherence degrades
   169→  (hallucination, contradiction, hedging).
   170→
   171→They are complementary, not redundant. An agent can be perfectly on-scope while
   172→its context quality degrades. Conversely, scope drift can happen with perfect
   173→context quality. Intent Checks continue firing alongside context-surfing's wave
   174→monitoring.
   175→
   176→**Precedence rule:** If both skills fire simultaneously (an Intent Check and a
   177→context-surfing drift exit at the same time), the drift exit takes precedence.
   178→Degraded context makes scope checks unreliable — resolve the context issue
   179→first, then resume scope monitoring in the next session.
   180→
   181→### What this skill produces
   182→
   183→- **Intent frame artifact** — consumed by context-surfing as part of the wave
   184→  anchor and copied verbatim into handoff files on drift exit.
   185→- **Intent resolution** — signals task completion, which triggers
   186→  simplify-and-harden.
   187→- **Drift observations** — scope drift patterns can be logged to
   188→  self-improvement as learnings if they recur.
   189→

1→---
     2→name: context-surfing
     3→description: >
     4→  Monitors context window health throughout a session and rides peak context quality for maximum output fidelity.
     5→  Activates automatically after plan-interview and intent-framed-agent. Stays active through execution and hands off
     6→  cleanly to simplify-and-harden and self-improvement when the wave completes naturally or exits via handoff.
     7→  Use this skill whenever a multi-step agent task is underway and session continuity or context drift is a concern.
     8→  Especially important for long-running tasks, complex refactors, or any work where degraded context would silently
     9→  corrupt the output. Trigger even if the user doesn't say "context surfing" — if an agent task is running across
    10→  multiple steps with intent and a plan already established, this skill is live.
    11→---
    12→
    13→# Context Surfing
    14→
    15→## Install
    16→
    17→```bash
    18→npx skills add pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills/skills/context-surfing
    19→```
    20→
    21→The agent rides the wave of peak context. When the wave crests, it commits. When it detects drift, it pulls out cleanly — saving state, handing off, and letting the next session catch the next wave.
    22→
    23→No wipeouts. No zombie sessions. Only intentional, high-fidelity execution.
    24→
    25→---
    26→
    27→## Mental Model
    28→
    29→Think of context like an ocean wave:
    30→
    31→- **Paddling in** = loading the intent frame, plan, and initial context. Energy is building.
    32→- **The peak** = full context coherence. The agent knows exactly what it's doing and why. This is when to execute.
    33→- **The shoulder** = context starting to flatten. Still rideable, but output density is dropping.
    34→- **The close-out** = drift. Contradiction, hedging, second-guessing, or hallucinated details. Wipe-out territory.
    35→
    36→The skill's job: ride as long as the wave is good, exit before it closes out.
    37→
    38→---
    39→
    40→## Lifecycle Position
    41→
    42→```
    43→[plan-interview] → [intent-framed-agent] → [context-surfing ACTIVE] → [simplify-and-harden] → [self-improvement]
    44→```
    45→
    46→Context Surfing is the execution layer. It wraps all work between intent capture and post-completion review. Simplify-and-harden and self-improvement are the next steps in the pipeline — they run after context-surfing completes, not as conditions that end it.
    47→
    48→### Relationship with intent-framed-agent
    49→
    50→Both skills are live during execution. They monitor different failure modes:
    51→
    52→- **intent-framed-agent** monitors *scope* drift — am I doing the right thing? It fires structured Intent Checks when work moves outside the stated outcome.
    53→- **context-surfing** monitors *context quality* drift — am I still capable of doing it well? It fires when the agent's own coherence degrades (hallucination, contradiction, hedging).
    54→
    55→They are complementary, not redundant. An agent can be perfectly on-scope while its context quality degrades (e.g., it's doing the right thing but starting to hallucinate details). Conversely, scope drift can happen with perfect context quality (the agent deliberately chases a tangent). Intent-framed-agent's Intent Checks continue firing alongside context-surfing's wave monitoring.
    56→
    57→**Precedence rule:** If both skills fire simultaneously (an Intent Check and a drift exit at the same time), context-surfing's exit takes precedence. Degraded context makes scope checks unreliable — resolve the context issue first, then resume scope monitoring in the next session.
    58→
    59→### When to Use the Full Pipeline
    60→
    61→Not every task needs all five skills. Match pipeline depth to task complexity:
    62→
    63→| Task Type | Skills to Use |
    64→|-----------|---------------|
    65→| Trivial (rename, typo fix) | None — just do it |
    66→| Small (isolated bug fix, single-file change) | `simplify-and-harden` only |
    67→| Medium (feature in known area, multi-file) | `intent-framed-agent` + `simplify-and-harden` |
    68→| Large (complex refactor, new architecture, unfamiliar codebase) | Full pipeline |
    69→| Long-running (multi-session, high context pressure) | Full pipeline with `context-surfing` as the critical skill |
    70→
    71→When in doubt, start light. Add skills if you notice drift or quality issues mid-task.
    72→
    73→---
    74→
    75→## Activation
    76→
    77→This skill is live the moment the intent frame and plan are established. No explicit invocation needed.
    78→
    79→At activation, load whatever anchors are available:
    80→
    81→1. The intent frame (from intent-framed-agent output) — if available
    82→2. The plan (from plan-interview output) — if available
    83→3. The current session state from the Entire CLI (if available)
    84→4. All project context files (see below)
    85→
    86→If neither an intent frame nor a plan exists (standalone mode), use the user's original task description combined with project context files as the wave anchor. This is sufficient — the skill degrades gracefully, not catastrophically.
    87→
    88→### Entire CLI Integration
    89→
    90→Entire CLI ([github.com/entireio/cli](https://github.com/entireio/cli)) provides persistent session state that serves as external ground truth for drift checks and handoff files.
    91→
    92→At activation, detect Entire:
    93→
    94→```bash
    95→entire status 2>/dev/null
    96→```
    97→
    98→- If it succeeds, use Entire as the session state backend. Log completions, in-progress items, and scope notes to it as work progresses.
    99→- If unavailable or failing, continue without it. Use the intent frame and plan file as the wave anchor instead. Track progress via structured comments in your output rather than Entire CLI commands. Do not block execution and do not nag about installation.
   100→
   101→The **wave anchor** is not held mentally. It is built from whatever external, persistent artifacts are available — every drift check reads from them directly, never from reconstructed memory.
   102→
   103→- **Full pipeline:** intent frame + plan file + Entire CLI session state
   104→- **Partial pipeline:** whichever of intent frame or plan exists, plus project context files
   105→- **Standalone:** the user's original task description + project context files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, README.md, etc.)
   106→
   107→The anchor is weaker in standalone mode — fewer artifacts to cross-check against — but it is always present. A weak anchor is better than no anchor.
   108→
   109→---
   110→
   111→## Project Context Files
   112→
   113→Before executing anything, scan the project for `.md` files that carry standing context. These are not documentation to skim — they are constraints, decisions, and architectural truth that must stay in the wave at all times.
   114→
   115→### Always load at activation
   116→- `CLAUDE.md` — agent configuration, conventions, constraints
   117→- `AGENTS.md` — multi-agent setup, role definitions
   118→- `README.md` — project intent and structure
   119→- Any `.md` in the project root
   120→
   121→### Load on demand (when relevant to the current task)
   122→- `.md` files in `skills/`, `docs/`, `.learnings/`, or similar directories
   123→- `SKILL.md` files for any skill being invoked alongside this one
   124→
   125→### Rules for context files
   126→1. **They are always part of the wave anchor.** If output contradicts a project `.md` file, that is a drift signal — treat it as a strong one.
   127→2. **Re-read them if the task changes domain or scope.** Don't assume you remembered correctly 20 steps in.
   128→3. **Include their key constraints in the handoff file.** The next session needs to reload them too — note which files were active and whether any were updated during the session.
   129→4. **If a `.md` file is modified during the session**, flag it explicitly in the handoff under a "Modified Context Files" section so the next session re-reads it fresh rather than relying on the handoff summary.
   130→
   131→---
   132→
   133→## Drift Detection
   134→
   135→Continuously monitor for these signals. Strong signals trigger an immediate exit — the wave is closing out. Weak signals trigger the Recovery Protocol first — the shoulder might still be rideable.
   136→
   137→### Strong signals (exit immediately)
   138→- The agent contradicts a decision it already made and committed to
   139→- A detail appears in the output that was never in the original context (hallucination)
   140→- The agent re-opens a scope question that was explicitly resolved in the plan
   141→- Output starts re-explaining the task rather than executing it
   142→
   143→### Weak signals (trigger recovery)
   144→- Responses are getting longer without getting more useful
   145→- Hedging language increases: "it depends", "could be", "might want to consider"
   146→- The agent switches approaches mid-task without explicit user direction
   147→- References to the original intent become vague or paraphrased instead of precise
   148→- The agent asks a clarifying question it should already know the answer to
   149→
   150→### Not drift
   151→- Normal iteration and refinement within scope
   152→- Asking about genuinely new information not in the original context
   153→- Simplifying a previous output (that's the wave working, not breaking)
   154→
   155→### The Monitoring Paradox
   156→
   157→An agent with degraded context is the least likely to detect its own degradation. The strong signals (hallucination, contradiction) are exactly the ones a compromised agent will miss — because it no longer has the context to recognize the contradiction.
   158→
   159→This is an inherent limitation of self-monitoring. Mitigate it with external grounding:
   160→
   161→1. **Re-read the wave anchor before each major step.** If an intent frame exists, open it and read it verbatim. If a plan file exists, re-read the relevant section. In standalone mode, re-read the user's original task description. Don't rely on your memory of any of these — open the artifact. If what you're about to do doesn't match what you read, stop.
   162→2. **Use Entire CLI logs as external memory.** If Entire is available, read back your own session log before non-trivial decisions. Your logged state is more reliable than your recalled state.
   163→3. **Treat the user as a drift sensor.** If the user expresses confusion, asks "why are you doing that?", or redirects you — treat it as a strong signal regardless of your own assessment.
   164→
   165→The weak signals (hedging, verbosity) are more reliably self-detectable precisely because they're behavioral, not factual. Watch for those as early warnings.
   166→
   167→### Recovery Protocol (Wave Re-Anchor)
   168→
   169→When weak signals accumulate, don't exit immediately — try to re-anchor first. The shoulder of the wave is still rideable if you can re-ground.
   170→
   171→#### Step 1: Pause and re-read
   172→
   173→Stop producing output. Re-read whatever wave anchor artifacts are available:
   174→
   175→1. If an intent frame exists, open and read it verbatim (not your memory of it)
   176→2. If a plan file exists, open and read the relevant section
   177→3. In standalone mode, re-read the user's original task description and project context files
   178→4. If Entire CLI is available, read back your session log
   179→
   180→Compare what you're currently doing against what these artifacts say you should be doing.
   181→
   182→#### Step 2: Reconcile
   183→
   184→- **If the mismatch resolves** — you can trace a clear line from the anchor to your current work — resume execution. The weak signals were noise, not drift.
   185→- **If uncertainty remains** — you can't confidently reconcile your current work with the anchor — escalate to the user. Present the situation openly: *"I'm noticing some drift. Here's where I am vs where the plan says I should be — how should I proceed?"* Include the specific weak signals you observed and what you found when you re-read the anchor.
   186→- **If the user re-grounds you** — integrate their clarification and resume. The re-anchor succeeded.
   187→- **If the user can't resolve it, or the original intent has fundamentally changed** — proceed to the Exit Protocol.
   188→
   189→#### Re-anchor limits
   190→
   191→There is no hard cap on recovery attempts. Keep re-anchoring as long as each attempt genuinely resolves the uncertainty and the user confirms alignment. However:
   192→
   193→- If you find yourself re-anchoring on consecutive steps, that is itself a weak signal — the wave is flattening and a natural exit may be close.
   194→- Strong signals always bypass recovery and trigger an immediate exit. Recovery is only for the shoulder, never for the close-out.
   195→
   196→---
   197→
   198→## Riding the Wave
   199→
   200→While context is healthy:
   201→
   202→1. **Execute with commitment.** No hedge, no re-litigating decisions already made. The plan is the plan.
   203→2. **Check the wave anchor before non-trivial decisions.** Re-read whatever anchor artifacts are available (intent frame, plan, or original task description). If the decision aligns, proceed. If it doesn't, stop.
   204→3. **Track completions.** Log what's done, what's in progress, what's pending as work progresses — not at exit. If Entire CLI is available, use it as the session log. If not, maintain a running status in your output. This feeds the handoff if needed.
   205→4. **Resist scope creep.** If something interesting but out-of-scope appears, note it (in Entire CLI or in your output) — don't chase it.
   206→
   207→---
   208→
   209→## Exit Protocol (Wave Close-Out)
   210→
   211→When a strong signal fires, or the Recovery Protocol fails to re-anchor, execute a clean exit. Do not try to push through.
   212→
   213→### Step 1: Stop executing
   214→
   215→Immediately pause task execution. Do not produce more output that may be corrupted by the degraded context.
   216→
   217→### Step 2: Write the handoff file
   218→
   219→Create a file named `.context-surfing/handoff-[slug]-[timestamp].md` (create the `.context-surfing/` directory if it doesn't exist). Add `.context-surfing/` to `.gitignore` — handoff files are session artifacts, not project history.
   220→
   221→Structure:
   222→
   223→```markdown
   224→# Context Surf Handoff
   225→
   226→## Session Info
   227→- Task: [task name / slug]
   228→- Started: [timestamp]
   229→- Ended: [timestamp]
   230→- Exit reason: [what drift signal was detected]
   231→
   232→## Intent Frame (if available — read verbatim, do not reconstruct)
   233→[copy directly from the intent-framed-agent artifact, or "N/A — standalone session" if none exists]
   234→
   235→## Plan (if available — read verbatim, do not reconstruct)
   236→[copy directly from the plan-interview artifact, or "N/A — standalone session" if none exists]
   237→
   238→## Original Task Description (standalone fallback)
   239→[copy the user's original task description if no intent frame or plan exists]
   240→
   241→## Completed Work (from Entire CLI session state or running output log)
   242→[pull directly from CLI log or structured output — do not reconstruct from memory]
   243→
   244→## In Progress at Exit (from Entire CLI session state or running output log)
   245→[what the session log shows as active at the moment of exit]
   246→[include any partial outputs if useful]
   247→
   248→## Pending Work (from plan-interview output — cross-reference session log to confirm what's genuinely not done)
   249→[remaining tasks from the plan, in order]
   250→
   251→## Drift Notes
   252→[what specifically triggered the exit — be precise, this helps the next session replan intelligently]
   253→
   254→## Active Context Files
   255→[list all .md files loaded during this session — root level and any skill/docs files consulted]
   256→
   257→## Modified Context Files
   258→[any .md files that were changed during this session — next session must re-read these, not trust the handoff summary]
   259→
   260→## Scope Notes (Out-of-Band)
   261→[anything interesting discovered that's outside scope — flagged for the next session to decide on]
   262→
   263→## Recommended Re-entry Point
   264→[where the next session should pick up, and any replanning it should do before continuing]
   265→```
   266→
   267→### Step 3: Notify the user
   268→
   269→Briefly and clearly:
   270→
   271→> "Context wave is done. I've saved the session state to `.context-surfing/[filename]`. The next session should load that file, run plan-interview to replan from [re-entry point], and catch the next wave. Here's what triggered the exit: [one sentence on drift signal]."
   272→
   273→Do not over-explain. The handoff file has the details.
   274→
   275→---
   276→
   277→## Handoff to Next Session
   278→
   279→The next session should:
   280→1. Read the handoff file completely before doing anything else
   281→2. If the original session used the full pipeline, run plan-interview using the handoff as input context and re-establish the intent frame via intent-framed-agent
   282→3. If the original session was standalone, use the handoff's original task description and drift notes to re-ground
   283→4. Pick up context-surfing again from the recommended re-entry point
   284→
   285→This is not failure. This is the system working correctly. Clean exits produce better total output than zombie sessions that limp to the finish line.
   286→
   287→---
   288→
   289→## Session Close (Natural Completion)
   290→
   291→When the task completes within a healthy wave (no drift exit needed):
   292→
   293→1. Confirm all plan items are done (or, in standalone mode, confirm the original task description is satisfied)
   294→2. Note session end in a brief summary (optional, not a full handoff file)
   295→3. Signal readiness for simplify-and-harden — the next skill in the pipeline picks up from here
   296→
   297→No handoff file needed for clean completions — just the outputs and a one-liner status.
   298→
   299→---
   300→
   301→## Interoperability with Other Skills
   302→
   303→### What this skill consumes
   304→- **From plan-interview (optional):** The plan file (`docs/plans/plan-NNN-<slug>.md`). Strengthens the wave anchor when available.
   305→- **From intent-framed-agent (optional):** The intent frame artifact. Strengthens the wave anchor when available.
   306→- **From the user (always available):** The original task description. Used as the standalone wave anchor when upstream artifacts are absent.
   307→- **From Entire CLI (optional):** Session state for progress tracking and external memory.
   308→
   309→### What this skill produces
   310→- **For simplify-and-harden:** A "ready" signal on natural completion. Simplify-and-harden picks up from the completed work.
   311→- **For the next session (on drift exit):** A handoff file in `.context-surfing/` with full state for session resumption.
   312→- **For self-improvement:** Drift patterns observed during the session can be logged as learnings if they recur.
   313→
   314→### Pipeline position
   315→1. `plan-interview` (optional, for requirement shaping)
   316→2. `intent-framed-agent` (execution contract + scope drift monitoring)
   317→3. `context-surfing` (context quality monitoring — runs concurrently with intent-framed-agent during execution)
   318→4. `simplify-and-harden` (post-completion quality/security pass)
   319→5. `self-improvement` (capture recurring patterns and promote durable rules)
   320→
   321→---
   322→
   323→## Hook Integration
   324→
   325→Enable automatic handoff detection at session start. This ensures handoff files from previous context exits are never silently ignored.
   326→
   327→### Setup (Claude Code / Codex)
   328→
   329→Add to `.claude/settings.json`:
   330→
   331→```json
   332→{
   333→  "hooks": {
   334→    "UserPromptSubmit": [{
   335→      "matcher": "",
   336→      "hooks": [{
   337→        "type": "command",
   338→        "command": "./skills/context-surfing/scripts/handoff-checker.sh"
   339→      }]
   340→    }]
   341→  }
   342→}
   343→```
   344→
   345→This checks for unread handoff files in `.context-surfing/` on every prompt. If found, it reminds the agent to read the handoff before starting new work (~100 tokens overhead, skips silently when no handoff exists).
   346→
   347→### Copilot / Chat Fallback
   348→
   349→For agents without hook support, manually check at session start:
   350→
   351→```bash
   352→ls .context-surfing/handoff-*.md 2>/dev/null
   353→```
   354→
   355→---
   356→
   357→## Principles
   358→
   359→**Ride the peak, not the whole ocean.** A shorter session with high fidelity beats a long session with gradual corruption.
   360→
   361→**Exit is not failure.** The wave close-out is a feature. Detecting it early is the skill.
   362→
   363→**The handoff file is the continuity.** It's not documentation overhead — it's what makes the next session as sharp as this one started.
   364→
   365→**Never hide the exit.** Always be explicit with the user that a context exit happened and why. Silently continuing in degraded context is the worst outcome.
   366→
